about: The Microprocessor Lab is Part IA Engineering coursework in Lent and Easter terms, linked to the 1P3 lecture course Digital Circuits and Information Processing; the 1P3 syllabus page (last modified December 2023) lists a 4-period experiment on PIC microprocessor programming and analogue interfacing. In the 2026-27 credit notice the Microprocessor course has 3 activities worth 2 marks each, awarded for prompt attendance and satisfactory work, under Part IA's standard-credit system. This guide explains the lab, its assessment and how to prepare; there is no separate syllabus beyond the 1P3 lectures and the lab handout.

notes.body:
The Microprocessor Lab is a piece of Part IA coursework in the Cambridge Engineering Tripos. The Department's Part IA syllabus index lists it among the "courses associated with coursework", running in Lent and Easter terms, with its handouts and resources on Moodle.

It is the practical partner of the 1P3 lecture course Digital Circuits and Information Processing. The 1P3 syllabus page (last modified December 2023, so check this year's version) lists the associated experimental work as:
- a 4-period experiment on PIC microprocessor programming and analogue interfacing;
- single-period ("short") experiments on combinational logic, and on sequential logic, memory and counting.

The 1P3 lectures are built around the Microchip PIC12F629/675 family of 8-pin microcontrollers, so expect the lab to use the same style of PIC assembly language: the working register W, file registers, bit-test-and-skip instructions and simple delay loops. Check your lab handout on Moodle for the exact hardware, software tools and tasks used this year, because these details are set by the lab leader and can change.

Why it matters
- It turns the lecture material on microprocessor architecture, registers, instruction sets and programme development into something you have actually done.
- Writing, assembling, downloading and debugging a real program makes ideas such as execution time in instruction cycles, conditional branches and input/output configuration far easier to remember for the Paper 3 exam.
- "Analogue interfacing" links the digital side of the course to the real world (for example reading a voltage or driving an output), which ties in with the D/A conversion and Schmitt-trigger material in 1P3.

There is no separate written exam on the lab itself. The material it practises is examinable through the 1P3 course in Part IA Paper 3 (Electrical and Information Engineering).

Assessment details below are taken from the Department's Coursework and Examination Credit Notice for Part IA (2026-27). Always check the current notice and your handout, as they are updated each year.

The Microprocessor course in the credit notice
- Terms: Lent and Easter.
- 3 activities, 2 marks each, so 6 marks in total.
- The qualifying mark is also 6.
- Each activity earns 2 marks for prompt attendance and satisfactory work, and 0 otherwise.

So there is no grading on a sliding scale here: you either complete each session properly and on time, or you lose the marks for it. Missing or arriving late to a session is the main way to lose credit.

How this fits into Part IA overall
- All Part IA coursework is for "standard credit": once you reach a satisfactory standard your raw marks are capped at the qualifying level.
- The maximum raw coursework mark across all Part IA coursework is 200 (the total qualifying mark). The final coursework mark is the raw total minus 100, so the maximum is 100, and most students are expected to receive it.
- The four written papers are each marked out of 200, and with the 100 coursework marks this gives a total of 900 for the Part IA examination.

What this means for you
- The lab is worth securing in full: the marks are easy to get with attendance and steady work, and hard to recover if lost.
- The intellectual payoff comes in Paper 3, where 1P3 questions can ask you to explain microprocessor operation, write short assembly sequences or work out execution times.

notes.h: PIC essentials to know before the lab
notes.body:
The 1P3 syllabus bases its programming examples on the PIC12F629/675. These facts come from Microchip's data sheet for that family and are worth having at your fingertips.

The device
- 8-pin microcontroller with a Harvard architecture: program memory and data memory are separate.
- 1024 words of flash program memory, 64 bytes of data RAM and 128 bytes of data EEPROM.
- 35 instructions; all are single-cycle except branches, which take two cycles.
- An 8-level hardware stack for subroutine return addresses.
- Six I/O pins, GP0 to GP5. GP3 is input only.
- The PIC12F675 adds a 10-bit analogue-to-digital converter with 4 input channels; the PIC12F629 has none. Both have one analogue comparator.
- Timer0 (8-bit) and Timer1 (16-bit), and an internal 4 MHz oscillator.

Timing
- One instruction cycle lasts four oscillator periods, so with a 4 MHz clock each single-cycle instruction takes 1 µs and a branch takes 2 µs.

Registers and instructions
- W is the working register. Most arithmetic and logic uses W and one file register f.
- The destination bit d chooses where the result goes: d = 0 puts it in W, d = 1 writes it back to f. For example ADDWF COUNT,F adds W to COUNT and stores the result in COUNT.
- Bit instructions: BSF and BCF set and clear one bit; BTFSS and BTFSC test a bit and skip the next instruction if it is set or clear. These are how you make decisions.
- TRISIO sets pin direction (1 = input, 0 = output) and GPIO holds the pin values. TRISIO lives in bank 1, so you select it with the RP0 bit of STATUS.

A standard delay loop
    MOVLW  D'250'
    MOVWF  COUNT
LOOP DECFSZ COUNT,F
    GOTO   LOOP
For N = 250 the loop runs 249 times at 3 cycles (DECFSZ 1 + GOTO 2), and the last DECFSZ takes 2 cycles when it skips. Adding the 2 set-up cycles gives 2 + 3 × 249 + 2 = 751 cycles, or 751 µs at 4 MHz. In general the total is 3N + 1 cycles.

notes.h: Preparing for and working in the lab
notes.body:
Before each session
- Read the handout on Moodle all the way through, and note what you must show a demonstrator to have the activity signed off.
- Revise binary and hexadecimal: you will set and test individual bits, so you need to translate quickly between 0x2F and 0010 1111.
- Re-read the 1P3 lecture notes on PIC architecture and the instruction set, and keep the instruction-set table from the data book next to you.
- Sketch your program on paper first: a flow chart or pseudo-code with the registers you will use and what each loop does.

During the session
- Arrive on time. In the credit notice, marks for this course depend on prompt attendance and satisfactory work.
- Build up in small steps: get a pin to change state first, then add the delay, then add input testing, then the analogue part.
- Comment every few lines of assembly. Comments such as "; wait for button on GP3" save time when debugging.
- When the program does not behave, check the usual suspects: wrong bank selected when writing TRISIO, a pin left configured as analogue or as a comparator input, the destination bit d (W or F) the wrong way round, and a skip instruction followed by the wrong line.
- Work out execution times by counting cycles, and check them against what you observe (for example with an oscilloscope if one is provided).

After the session
- Write a short summary of what each instruction you used does, with one example. This becomes a revision sheet for the PIC part of 1P3.
- Practise past Paper 3 questions on microprocessors: explaining how instructions are executed, designing address decoders, and calculating loop timings are the skills the lab rehearses.

Exam tips: be able to write a 5–10 line PIC routine from memory, explain the role of W, STATUS and TRISIO, and count instruction cycles accurately, remembering that skips and GOTOs take two cycles.

questions.q: According to the 2026-27 Part IA credit notice, how are marks awarded for each Microprocessor course activity?
options: 2 marks for prompt attendance and satisfactory work, 0 otherwise
A mark out of 6 based on the quality of a written report
A mark out of 10 from a short test at the end of the session
No marks: the lab is purely formative
questions.why: The notice lists 3 activities at 2 marks each, awarded for prompt attendance and satisfactory work, otherwise 0. There is no graded report or test, and the activities do carry marks (6 in total, qualifying mark 6).

questions.q: A PIC12F675 runs from its 4 MHz internal oscillator. How long does the instruction sequence MOVLW D'100' / MOVWF C / LOOP DECFSZ C,F / GOTO LOOP take?
questions.why: Total cycles = 2 (set-up) + 3 × 99 (DECFSZ 1 + GOTO 2 on each non-final pass) + 2 (final DECFSZ that skips) = 301 cycles = 3N + 1. Each cycle is 4 clock periods = 1 µs, so 301 µs. 300 µs counts 3 cycles for all 100 passes and forgets the 2 set-up cycles (and that the last pass is a 2-cycle skip with no GOTO); 400 µs takes DECFSZ as 2 cycles, giving 4 per pass (2 + 4 × 99 + 2); 202 µs takes GOTO as a single cycle, giving 2 per pass (2 + 2 × 99 + 2).

questions.q: A student writes MOVLW B'00000000' then MOVWF TRISIO while bank 0 is selected. What is the most likely problem?
options: TRISIO is in bank 1, so the write goes to a different register; RP0 must be set first
TRISIO bits of 0 make every pin an input
MOVWF cannot write to special function registers
MOVLW cannot load the value zero
questions.why: On the PIC12F629/675 TRISIO sits in bank 1, selected by setting RP0 in STATUS; with bank 0 selected the same address refers to another register. A 0 in TRISIO makes a pin an output, not an input; MOVWF can write any file register; and MOVLW can load 0.

questions.q: Explain why execution times of PIC assembly routines can be calculated exactly, and calculate the delay produced by a single DECFSZ/GOTO loop loaded with N = 200 on a 4 MHz PIC12F675.
markScheme: Every instruction takes a fixed number of instruction cycles: one, or two for branches/skips
One instruction cycle is 4 oscillator periods = 1 µs at 4 MHz
questions.modelAnswer: The PIC executes a fixed instruction set in which every instruction takes a known number of instruction cycles: one for most instructions, two for GOTO, CALL, returns and a skip that is taken. There is no cache, and the effect of the PIC's simple two-stage fetch/execute pipeline is already built into the two-cycle timing of branches, so counting instructions gives the exact time. Each instruction cycle is four oscillator periods, i.e. 1 µs at 4 MHz. For MOVLW N, MOVWF C, then LOOP: DECFSZ C,F; GOTO LOOP: the set-up takes 2 cycles; the loop body runs N − 1 times at 3 cycles; the final DECFSZ reaches zero and skips, taking 2 cycles. Total = 2 + 3(N − 1) + 2 = 3N + 1. For N = 200 this is 601 cycles, so the delay is 601 µs.
